messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet was fifteen when the fighting reached his village in the central highlands. He remembers the day not as a sequence of events but as a series of explosions—sound that tore through the air before his brain could register what it meant. He had been walking back from the river with his younger sister, Lan, when the first mortar struck the market. The blast threw them both to the ground. In the chaos that followed, Kiet dragged Lan toward the tree line, but she was hit again—shrapnel, he later learned—and she stopped moving. He tried to lift her, but his arms gave out. He stayed there, holding her hand, until a neighbor pulled him away. He was fourteen. By the time he reached a refugee camp three weeks later, he had stopped speaking about it. No one asked.

Now, at eighteen, Kiet lives in a small apartment in a Midwestern city and works as a photographer—mostly portrait sessions and the occasional wedding. The job pays enough, but it has become a source of constant strain. Ordinary sounds like a door slamming or a car backfiring make him jump, his heart hammering before his mind catches up. He finds himself scanning rooms for exits, for anything that could be a threat, even when he knows he is safe. At a wedding shoot last month, the pop of a champagne cork sent him diving behind a table. The bride laughed it off, but Kiet felt the familiar wash of shame and something else—anger, hot and sharp, because the memory had come without warning: the mortar, the dust, Lan’s face. The memory feels more real than the present moment, vivid and unforgiving, and when it returns he feels an intense rage that has nowhere to go.

Kiet has come to believe that he no longer belongs anywhere. In the camp, he learned that people cannot be trusted—aid workers who promised food and delivered nothing, older boys who stole his blanket. Now, in the city, he keeps everyone at arm’s length. He is certain that he should have protected Lan, and that he failed. That failure sits at the center of everything, a judgment he cannot shake. It makes him mistrustful of anyone who offers help, because he believes he does not deserve it. It also makes him hypervigilant: he scans the faces of strangers on the street for signs of danger, because if he lets his guard down, he might fail again. This constant watchfulness, this inability to relax, means his nerves are always frayed. And when he is on edge, the memories come more easily—a shard of sound, a flash of movement, and he is back in the highlands. Each memory, in turn, reinforces his belief that he failed. He remembers Lan’s hand going limp, and the rage and guilt spiral together until he feels like he is drowning.

The cycle has tightened over the past year. Kiet has begun taking risks that worry even him. He accepted a job photographing a demolition site, standing close to collapsing walls, telling himself it didn’t matter if something fell. He has started driving without his seatbelt, accelerating through yellow lights. He knows this is dangerous, but a part of him feels that he is already damaged, already unreachable, so what difference does it make? This risky behavior is the one thing that quiets the hypervigilance for a moment—the adrenaline overriding the constant scanning. But it also feeds his mistrust of himself: if he behaves this recklessly, he really cannot be trusted. And that makes him feel even more isolated, more certain that he doesn’t belong among ordinary people.

He has not told anyone about any of this. His few acquaintances know him as quiet, occasionally jumpy, a little intense. But last week, during a portrait session, the click of his camera shutter—a sound he has heard thousands of times—suddenly triggered a full memory of the mortar blast. He dropped the camera and stood frozen, his hands shaking, while the client stared. He could not finish the session. That night, he searched online for help. What frightens him most is the feeling that he is losing control—that the rage and the sudden memories and the reckless urges are all converging, and that one day he will do something he cannot undo. He hopes that someone can tell him how to stop the cycle, but a deeper part of him is certain that no one can.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals causally lead to memory; the link is indirect via threat.
No paragraph conveys that threat causally leads to negative appraisals; the connection is missing.
